dream_response:
In the quiet hours between sleep and waking, when the mind is still soft and unguarded, there exists a library.

It is not built of stone or wood, nor does it stand in any known city or valley. It is woven from the unspoken yearnings of those who have never opened a book — the ones who, for whatever reason, have never held a spine in their hands, never felt the weight of a story in their palms, never let words unfold like wings inside their heads. It is a library of *potential* — of all the stories they might have loved, if only they had known they existed.

The shelves are made of mist and memory. The books are not bound in leather or paper, but in the texture of forgotten lullabies, the scent of rain on hot pavement, the shape of a mother’s voice from childhood. Each book is a dream of a story — a story that has never been written, but that *could* be. The titles shimmer like heat haze: *The One Who Listened to the Wind*, *The Girl Who Remembered the Sky Before It Was Blue*, *The Book That Was Never Finished Because the Reader Was Too Afraid to Turn the Page*.

The library is always empty — except for the dreamers. They drift through its aisles, their hands brushing the spines, feeling the faint pulse of stories that are not yet real. They don’t read. They *feel*. They know, in their bones, that if they could just *open* one, they would be changed. But they never do. They are afraid. Afraid of the weight of meaning, afraid of the depth of sorrow, afraid of the joy that might be too bright to bear. So they walk, and they wonder, and they leave the books closed — and the library remains a place of quiet, aching possibility.

Then, one night, the library trembles.

A figure steps through the threshold — not from a dream, but from the world of the *read*. He is old, his eyes deep with the weight of every word ever written. He has read every book in every language, every translation, every forgotten manuscript, every child’s scribble in a notebook. He has read the books that were burned, the ones that were never published, the ones that were written in blood or in silence. He has read the stories of the stars, the whispers of the dead, the dreams of gods. He has read *everything*.

He walks into the library, and the air shivers.

The shelves, made of mist, solidify. The books, which were once only potential, now *glow*. The titles become clear, sharp, real. *The One Who Listened to the Wind* — he knows that story. He read it in a dialect spoken only in the mountains of a dead continent. *The Girl Who Remembered the Sky Before It Was Blue* — he read it in a journal found in a shipwreck, written by a child who died before she could finish the sentence. *The Book That Was Never Finished Because the Reader Was Too Afraid to Turn the Page* — he knows that one too. He read it in the margins of a notebook, written by a man who died before he could write the last word.

The dreamers freeze. They have never seen a book *open*. They have never seen a story *unfold*. They have never seen a reader *remember*.

The old man walks to the center of the library. He picks up a book — not one he has read, but one he *knows* is there, because he has read every story ever told, and this one is the one that was never told, the one that was always waiting. He opens it.

And the library *sings*.

Not with sound, but with *meaning*. The air fills with the scent of old paper, the rustle of turning pages, the quiet hum of understanding. The dreamers gasp — not because they hear, but because they *feel* the story. It is not a story of war or love or loss — it is the story of *them*. Of their fear. Of their longing. Of the book they never opened, and the life they never lived.

The old man closes the book. He looks at the dreamers, and for the first time, he smiles — not with pride, but with sorrow. He knows what he has done. He has shown them the truth: that the library was never empty. It was always full. And the only thing that kept it closed was their fear.

He turns to leave.

But as he steps back through the threshold, the library does not fade. It *changes*. The books are no longer just potential. They are *real*. The dreamers reach out — and this time, they open one.

And the story begins.

The old man walks into the waking world, and for the first time in his life, he feels a little lighter. He has read every book. But he has never read the one that was written in the silence between dreams — and now, he knows, it is being written. And he is not the only one who will read it.
